newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia, Khmer Rouge dissidents still apart.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia, Khmer Rouge dissidents still apart.

text.p: Cambodian co-premier Hun Sen's recent meeting with dissident Khmer Rouge leaders narrowed the gap between the two sides but analysts and officials say key differences need to be tackled at upcoming high-level talks.
Hun Sen on Monday held his first direct talks with several leaders of the dissident group which last month broke away from Pol Pot's hardline Khmer Rouge.
Hun Sen said requests by representatives of Ieng Sary -- leader of the breakaway faction -- were not extravagant and said he viewed the meeting as successful.
"They asked for two things -- firstly to join the government troops step-by-step and, secondly, to grant amnesty to Ieng Sary," Hun Sen said after the meeting in western Cambodia.
Analysts said key sticking points appear to be integration of the territory controlled by the breakaway faction into government hands and the question of what to do with Ieng Sary.

Ieng Sary, now in his 60s and a former Khmer Rouge foreign minister, was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in systematic killings by the guerrilla group when it ruled Cambodia from April 1975 to December 1978.
More than one million people died of disease, starvation or execution during the Khmer Rouge's reign of terror.
The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-brokered Cambodia peace pact in 1991, but reneged on the accord and have been fighting the coalition that emerged from general elections in 1993.

Ieng Sary supporters control at least two major strongholds in northwestern Phnom Malai and neighbouring Pailin areas. Cambodian officials said the momentum in negotiations with the dissidents would continue with a planned first meeting on Thursday between the elusive Ieng Sary and co-Defence Ministers Tea Banh and Tea Chamrath.
Analysts believed such a meeting could pave the way for talks between Ieng Sary and co-Premiers Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
But the exact location or timing of the planned meeting between the Cambodian defence chiefs and Ieng Sary at his sanctuary somewhere around Phnom Malai was unclear.
Tea Chamrath told Reuters he and Tea Banh were going to Bangkok on Wednesday but declined to detail his schedule.
Information Minister Ieng Mouly said things would be clearer after talks between the defence chiefs and Ieng Sary.
"I think the process is accelerating...I think there will be some solution in the near future," he told Reuters.
"The problem may be over the Ieng Sary role."
Hun Sen on Monday called for Ieng Sary to be granted a royal pardon.
Ieng Sary has said he is setting up a group called the Democratic National United Movement to work for peace and reconciliation with Cambodia.

A Western diplomat believed Monday's meeting between Hun Sen and the dissidents led by Ieng Vuth, son of Ieng Sary, was significant, especially if the dissidents were more interested in discussing territory arrangements.
"It does seem to be going well. Relations seem to be solidifying," he said.
Another analyst was not so upbeat but said talks between Ieng Sary and the ministers "will be a step up -- definitely progress, when you get face-to-face with the principals."
But rivalries within the Cambodian government seemed to affect talks with the Khmer Rouge dissidents, the analyst said.
Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party and the royalist FUNCINPEC of Ranariddh, have had some political differences over power-sharing.
FUNCINPEC parliamentary minister Ahmad Yahya said Hun Sen should have met Ieng Sary, along with representatives of the FUNCINPEC, as requested by the dissidents.
"I'm pessimistic about the negotiations," he said. "There were a lot of demands from their side and I don't think the government will fulfill all their demands."
